title: Vashu Bhagnani Has Filed a ₹400 Crore Lawsuit Over Chunari Chunari. The Case Could Rewrite Bollywood's Music Rights Playbook.
excerpt: The Biwi No.1 producer alleges Tips Industries and David Dhawan recreated his iconic songs without consent. Tips says it owns the rights. The Bombay High Court will decide who is right — and the answer will affect every remake in the industry.
body:
The song Chunari Chunari was released in 1999 as part of the Biwi No.1 soundtrack. It became a wedding staple, a garba-night anthem, and one of those rare Bollywood tracks that transcended its film to become a permanent fixture of Indian cultural life — in India and across the diaspora. Twenty-seven years later, it is at the centre of a legal battle that could reshape how Bollywood handles its most valuable asset: old music.

Vashu Bhagnani, the producer of Biwi No.1, has filed a ₹400 crore lawsuit before the Bombay High Court against Tips Industries, its promoters Ramesh Taurani and Kumar S Taurani, and filmmaker David Dhawan. At the centre of the dispute: the recreation of Chunari Chunari and another track, Ishq Sona Hai, in the new Varun Dhawan-starrer Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai, which released on June 5.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=abNAyUX0Oqw</youtube>


## The Core Dispute

The legal question is deceptively simple. Tips Industries holds the audio rights to the original Biwi No.1 soundtrack. That much is not contested. What Bhagnani argues is that audio rights and recreation rights are legally distinct — and that recreating the song for a new film, with new singers and a new arrangement, required his consent as the original film's producer, since the intellectual property of the film itself (including visual associations, cultural identity, and the creative context of the song) belongs to him.

Tips Industries has rejected the allegation. Its position is that ownership of audio rights includes the right to license recreations and remakes, and that Bhagnani's consent was neither legally required nor contractually stipulated.

If the Bombay High Court rules in Bhagnani's favour, the implications would extend far beyond this one case. Bollywood's remake economy — which has turned old songs into a reliable revenue stream through recreations in new films — could face a fundamental reordering. Producers of original films might suddenly hold veto power over remakes of songs they funded, even when the audio rights were sold decades ago.

## The Personal Dimension

The lawsuit is not merely legal. It is personal.

Bhagnani held a virtual press conference in which he spoke about the breakdown of his relationship with Varun Dhawan, who starred in his 2020 production Coolie No. 1. The film reportedly resulted in a ₹27 crore loss. According to Bhagnani, Varun has not contacted him in two years. "He is like my child," Bhagnani said. "Children make mistakes. Father and son, so be it."

Varun, for his part, appeared on Farah Khan's YouTube show on the same day the lawsuit was filed. When he arrived late, Farah asked if he had been to meet "Vashu ji." Varun smiled and said: "That's what I went to handle." The exchange went viral, with viewers reading between the lines. Whether the quip was a deflection or a power move, it confirmed that the industry is watching this dispute closely.

## What This Means for Remakes

Bollywood's relationship with its own back catalogue has always been commercially pragmatic and legally murky. The 2012 Copyright Amendment Act strengthened the rights of authors and composers, but the treatment of producers' rights in the context of song recreations remains a grey area. Most remake deals are negotiated between music labels and production houses without involving the original film's producer — a practice that has gone largely unchallenged because most legacy producers either lack the resources to fight or have moved on.

Bhagnani is neither. He has the resources, and he has not moved on.

The outcome of this case will be watched closely by producers, music labels, and anyone involved in Bollywood's thriving remake economy. If the court establishes that film producers retain a separate, distinct right over the recreation of songs from their films — independent of whoever holds the audio rights — the cost and complexity of every song remake in the industry will increase overnight.

## The Diaspora Context

For NRI audiences, Chunari Chunari is not just a film song. It is the soundtrack of sangeet nights, Navratri celebrations, and wedding playlists that have not changed in a generation. The question of who owns the right to remake it — and under what terms — touches something deeper than copyright law. It touches cultural inheritance.

The case is pending before the Bombay High Court. Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai, meanwhile, has collected approximately ₹15 crore in its first two days, with the disputed songs intact. Whether they stay in the film will depend on what the court decides next.
